\chapter{Where -er and -ir Part Company}
\label{ch:spanish-er-ir-1pl}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what we eat and what we live, and explain why the singular hid the difference.}

comemos and vivimos: one vowel apart, audible only because the ending is stressed.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comemos]{comemos — \textquotedblleft{}we eat\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-comemos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablamos}.) And \textquotedblleft{}I eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Como}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same -mos, a different vowel}]
Drop the \textbf{-er}, add \textbf{-emos}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{comemos} — \emph{we eat.}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{-mos} is the one you already have from \emph{hablamos}. Only the vowel in front of it changed, from \textbf{a} to \textbf{e} — and it changed for the reason it always does: the ending takes the colour of its family.

That is the pattern for every plural ending you will meet. \textbf{-mos} and \textbf{-n} never change. The vowel before them does.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Something is about to happen that has not happened before.} In the singular, \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} were \textbf{identical} — \emph{como/comes/come} and \emph{vivo/vives/vive}, the same three endings twice over. That was a genuine saving, and it is about to stop. The next lesson is where the two families finally part.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}hablamos\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}comemos\textquotedblright{} — the same \emph{-mos}, a different vowel
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}we eat\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Comemos}.) Which part of a plural ending never changes? (The \textbf{-mos}.) And what has been true of \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} until now? (They were \textbf{identical} — which the next lesson ends.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vivimos]{vivimos — where the two families part}

\label{lesson:ES-C07-vivimos}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}we eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Comemos}.) And \textquotedblleft{}I live.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Vivo}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the saving ends here}]
Drop the \textbf{-ir}, add \textbf{-imos}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{vivimos} — \emph{we live.}
\end{quote}

Not \emph{vivemos}. \textbf{Vivimos}.

This is the first form in the whole book where \emph{-er} and \emph{-ir} do not match. For every singular form you learned, the two families shared endings exactly — and you were told that saving would end in the plural. This is where.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{comemos} — we eat.  ·  \textbf{vivimos} — we live.
\end{quote}

One vowel apart, and it is each family's own vowel: the \textbf{e} of \emph{comer}, the \textbf{i} of \emph{vivir}. The families were never really the same; the singular endings simply happened to fall out identically.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Why did the singular hide the difference and the plural expose it?

Stress. In \emph{vivo}, \emph{vives}, \emph{vive}, the stress is on the \textbf{stem} and the ending is unstressed — and unstressed vowels wear toward each other until they are indistinguishable. In \emph{vivimos}, the stress lands on the \textbf{ending itself}, and a stressed vowel keeps its own quality.

So the families did not diverge here. They were always distinct, and the plural is simply the place where the stress lets you hear it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}comemos\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}vivimos\textquotedblright{} — and hear the one vowel that separates them
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}we live\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Vivimos}.) Why was the difference invisible in the singular? (The ending was \textbf{unstressed}, so the vowels wore together.) And what makes it audible here? (The \textbf{stress} falls on the ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
